Reranking a hypothetical pool of `{python} RerankPool.pool_str` candidates of `{python} RerankPool.passage_str` tokens each against a `{python} RerankPool.query_str`-token query processes `{python} RerankPool.total_str` tokens for one query, as much prefill as a substantial model call, spent only on ordering. The runtime controls that cost by shrinking the pool, reranking only when the next decision warrants the precision, or running the reranker off the interactive path. @Fig-vol3-hnsw-rrf assembles the whole read path, from the two candidate lists to the staged set.

::: {#fig-vol3-hnsw-rrf fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Candidate Lists to Staged Evidence**: Lexical and dense retrieval each rank candidates for the repair symptom. Candidates are joined on their full identity, so an r17 span never merges with its r18 counterpart, and reciprocal rank fusion combines ranks rather than raw scores, with the smoothing parameter $k_{\text{rrf}}$ still a design choice. A cross-encoder reorders only a short pool, because its work grows with both pool size and pair length, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget." fig-alt="Vertical flowchart. A query box quoting the symptom a connection is returned, but another caller keeps waiting branches to two boxes, lexical ranking (BM25) and dense retrieval (ANN). Both merge into a box labeled join on candidate identity, noting scope, path, version, and span. Arrows continue to reciprocal rank fusion with its reciprocal-rank formula, then to a cross-encoder reranker over a short pool, and finally to a box labeled stage a small set within the payload budget."}
![](images/svg/vol3_ch06_hnsw_rrf.svg)
:::

Finally, the ordered candidates still have to become usable evidence. The runtime applies the retrieval contract's bound scope, permissions, and source-version requirements, and selects excerpts within the serialized payload budget. It preserves provenance and reports truncation. The agent must then assess what those excerpts support. Finding the `r18` implementation and a passing reproducer supports a narrower claim than showing that every caller behaves correctly. The next question is how to retrieve the related records needed for such a broader claim, using further queries or maintained relationships when those methods are useful.

## Multi-Hop Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-graphrag}

A ranked passage can identify where to begin without supplying everything needed for the next decision. In the connection-pool repair, the implementation, the waiter/return test, and the recorded test outcome answer different questions. The implementation alone leaves open what the test exercised, and the passing result alone leaves open whether the public interface survived. **Multi-hop retrieval**\index{Multi-hop retrieval!definition} follows relationships among evidence items, assembling an explanation that no single item's query score supplies.

Multi-hop retrieval needs no graph database. An agent can read a passage, identify a relevant reference, and request the next source through a bounded tool. The runtime can also follow known links before calling the model. The design choice is between discovering relationships on demand and maintaining them, which pays only when repeated questions reuse relationships whose extraction cost can be amortized.

### Following an evidence path

For the repair, a useful retrieval path starts at the recorded failure and follows its provenance into the code under investigation. Locating the `r17` failure record for `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, including the test revision and configuration, identifies an observed failure under those specific conditions rather than a failure of every later revision. Reading the corresponding test in `tests/test_pool.py` then follows the pool operations referenced by its controlled waiter/return scenario into the relevant regions of `src/pool.py` at the tested revision. Finally, comparing those regions with the `r18` candidate and its recorded reproducer result evaluates the candidate fix, keeping the passing result scoped to the executed test while leaving interface guarantees and relevant callers to be inspected separately.

The links in this path have different meanings. A test record's source-version link identifies the artifact it observed. A reference in test code identifies a symbol to inspect. A comparison between revisions identifies a change. Collapsing all three into an unlabeled association would conceal the reasoning that connects the failure, patch, and result.

A retrieval response should therefore preserve the relationships that made the returned items useful, along with their source locations and versions. It should also expose unresolved links: an unavailable test log, an ambiguous call target, or a read stopped by a budget. A connected path locates candidates for a root cause; it records neither that the calls executed in the failing run nor that the path is complete.

### Maintaining links for repeated questions

A simple structural index may contain symbol definitions and references. A **code property graph**\index{Code property graph!definition} combines richer representations of syntax, control flow, and dependencies [@yamaguchi2014modeling]. These structures can support queries such as locating callers or following reads of a shared field. They complement lexical and dense search: an exact symbol lookup, a ranked passage, or a known source location can all supply a starting node, called a seed.

The graph's data model is what makes "follow the right links" precise. A code property graph is a directed multigraph $G=(V,E,\Sigma_V,\Sigma_E,\mu_V,\mu_E)$. Its vertices $V$ are program entities typed by $\Sigma_V$ (file, module, class, function, variable), and each edge in $E$ carries a type from an alphabet $\Sigma_E$. The attribute maps $\mu_V$ and $\mu_E$ attach properties such as source spans, source generations, and call-site locations. Five edge families carry most repository questions. Containment and declaration edges (`CONTAINS`, `DECLARES`) come from the syntax tree; invocation edges (`CALLS`) link call sites to targets; data-dependence edges (`READS`, `MODIFIES`, `REACHES`) follow values between definitions and uses; type edges (`INHERITS`, `IMPLEMENTS`) resolve hierarchies; and module edges (`IMPORTS`) link files. The original formulation merges the syntax tree, the control-flow graph, and the program-dependence graph into this one structure. In the repair, a traversal permitted only `CALLS` and `MODIFIES` edges can go from `test_waiter_notified_on_return` to the pool's return method and on to the waiter set that method changes, without collecting every file that merely imports the pool.

The usefulness of an edge depends on how it was obtained. Parsing can recover declared structure; resolving cross-file calls may need types, build configuration, or additional analysis. Dynamic dispatch and generated code can leave targets uncertain. An observed execution trace supplies different evidence and covers only the execution recorded. The graph should retain these distinctions rather than turn every inferred relation into an observed event. The edge attributes $\mu_E$ carry that distinction by recording whether each edge came from parsing, from resolution under a stated build configuration, or from a recorded trace.

Maintaining those links costs work when sources change. A local edit may affect callers or summaries outside the changed file, while an unrelated edit leaves the edges intact. A retrieval policy needs the applicable source versions and a way to exclude or label relationships whose support has changed, the update contract that @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation develops.

Two tiers of extraction keep that cost tractable. A syntactic parser re-parses an edited file locally, in time proportional to the file, and recovers declarations, spans, and imports but not resolved cross-file calls. Compiler-grade extraction resolves types and call targets across the whole build, which requires rerunning whole-program analysis and is slow on a large repository. A tiered design keeps the compiler-grade graph as a base and overlays a local delta from the fast parser, serving the view $G_{\text{view}}=(G_{\text{global}}\setminus T)\cup \Delta G_{\text{local}}$, where $T$ holds the base graph's vertices and edges from the edited files. The overlay's edges carry parse-level evidence until the background pass replaces them, and $\mu_E$ says so.

### Bounding expansion and staged evidence

Following every relation from a seed can collect far more material than the model should receive. Expansion needs limits on permitted edge types, direction, depth, visited nodes, and search work. Tracking visited node identities prevents cycles and overlapping paths from producing repeated expansion. These traversal limits do not replace the final payload budget: a small number of large nodes can still exceed the available context.

The runtime can prioritize candidates by task relevance, relation type, or a graph score. Personalized PageRank is one optional ranking method that biases graph exploration toward designated seeds; the repository-map formulation is in @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pagerank. A score threshold selects high-scoring nodes, which may still be disconnected, insufficient as evidence, or too large for the token allowance. Selecting a useful path may require retaining a low-ranked intermediate node and spending fewer tokens elsewhere.

The expansion example below separates the number of reachable candidates from the number that can be staged. Its tree is deliberately simple enough to count exactly.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context.
# │ Goal: Separate a traversal neighborhood from a serialized packing bound.
# │ Show: 40 reachable nodes require 7,300 tokens; at most 33 fit in 6,144.
# │ How: Count an exact tree, then apply a hypothetical final-serialization budget.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int

class GraphNeighborhoodExpansion:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    call_tokens = 32_768
    output_tokens = 2_048
    other_input_tokens = 24_576
    children = 3  # exact tree: every internal node has this many children
    depth = 3  # seed is depth zero; no repeated nodes
    node_tokens = 180  # fixed serialized size, including local provenance
    edge_envelope_tokens = 100  # stipulated total for either packing considered

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Integer token accounting) ─────────────────────────────────
    allowance = call_tokens - output_tokens - other_input_tokens
    nodes = (children ** (depth + 1) - 1) // (children - 1)
    required = nodes * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens
    fit = (allowance - edge_envelope_tokens) // node_tokens
    packed = fit * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens
    shallow_nodes = (children**depth - 1) // (children - 1)  # one level less
    shallow_required = shallow_nodes * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(allowance == 6_144, "Match the chapter's retrieval allowance")
    check(nodes == 40 and required == 7_300, "Include seed and every level")
    check(fit == 33 and packed <= allowance, "Packing must fit")
    check(packed + node_tokens > allowance, "One more complete node cannot fit")
    check(required > allowance, "Full neighborhood exceeds the payload budget")
    check(shallow_nodes == 13 and shallow_required == 2_440 <= allowance, "One level shallower fits")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    children_str = fmt_int(children)
    depth_str = fmt_int(depth)
    nodes_str = fmt_int(nodes)
    node_tokens_str = fmt_int(node_tokens)
    edge_tokens_str = fmt_int(edge_envelope_tokens)
    allowance_str = fmt_int(allowance)
    required_str = fmt_int(required)
    fit_str = fmt_int(fit)
    shallow_depth_str = fmt_int(depth - 1)
    shallow_nodes_str = fmt_int(shallow_nodes)
    shallow_required_str = fmt_int(shallow_required)
```

::: {#nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context .callout-notebook title="Graph expansion and the evidence budget"}

**Problem**: Can the complete neighborhood around one seed fit the chapter's `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.allowance_str`-token retrieval allowance?

**Variables**: Suppose the neighborhood is a tree with exactly `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.children_str` children per internal node, explored through depth `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.depth_str`, with the seed at depth zero and no repeated nodes. Each complete node record occupies `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.node_tokens_str` serialized tokens, including its local provenance. Reserve `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.edge_tokens_str` tokens total for edge descriptions and the result envelope. All counts are hypothetical fixed serialization sizes.

**Math**: Counting the seed and all levels gives $1 + 3 + 9 + 27 =$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.nodes_str` nodes. Staging them requires `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.nodes_str` $\times$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.node_tokens_str` $+$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.edge_tokens_str` $=$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.required_str` tokens, exceeding the allowance. With the same envelope reservation, the maximum number of complete equal-sized nodes is $\lfloor(6{,}144 - 100)/180\rfloor =$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.fit_str`.

Stopping one level earlier, at depth `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.shallow_depth_str`, stages all `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.shallow_nodes_str` nodes in `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.shallow_required_str` tokens.

**Systems insight**: Depth is the knob that moves the result, because each level multiplies the frontier by the branching factor: one level separates a neighborhood that fits with room to spare from one that overflows. Bound depth and permitted edge types first, then let ranking choose among the nodes the budget can hold, keeping the low-ranked intermediate nodes that connect the evidence. The packing bound counts what fits; which records suffice is the ranking's job, measured on the final serialization.

:::

Real graphs can have overlapping neighborhoods, cycles, and uneven degrees. A mean branching factor raised to a depth approximates, and usually overstates, their distinct reachable nodes, and search may inspect many candidates it never stages. The response must distinguish an exhausted search space under its declared semantics from a traversal stopped by a limit. When the evidence path does not fit, the runtime can narrow the question, return a bounded subset with continuation information, or obtain further evidence in a later call, and in every case it reports the omitted path as unchecked.

### Community summaries as derived memory {#sec-vol3-graphrag-hierarchical}

Some information needs concern a subsystem rather than one path. A question about how connection management, request handling, and tests fit together may benefit from an overview before detailed reads. GraphRAG is one approach that builds an entity graph and precomputes summaries of related communities for broader questions [@edge2024graphrag]. Community detection supplies a grouping; whether a group matches a software responsibility, and whether its summary is correct, remain separate questions.

A summary can reduce repeated reading, but it is a new, lossy record. It needs links to its supporting material, the versions and scope it describes, and permissions appropriate to the information it contains. A summary spanning several sources carries the access restrictions of its most restricted source. Detailed decisions open the supporting records; the overview only points to them.

For example, a repair summary may record that the `r18` candidate passed `test_waiter_notified_on_return` under a stated configuration while broader compatibility remains unverified. It must not silently become “the connection pool is correct.” A later change to the relevant implementation or test can remove its support for a current-state claim while the historical test result stays true. Creating summaries also creates a maintenance obligation: identify affected derivatives when support changes, and revise, withdraw, or retain them explicitly as history under the record's policy. Recording which communities and sources each summary covers makes the first step mechanical, since a change marks every dependent summary, and every summary built from those, dirty; a dirty summary may still be served as a labeled historical view until it is regenerated.

::: {#chk-06-hybrid-retrieval .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing and bounding related evidence"}

Apply the retrieval choices to the continuing repair.

- [ ] **Method choice**: A query supplies an exact test identifier, but the next question concerns related callers. Which reads or indexes could support each step, and when would maintaining a graph justify its cost?
- [ ] **Evidence path**: Why does a static path from the test to an implementation not establish the observed root cause or broader correctness of `r18`?
- [ ] **Expansion estimate**: In the notebook's tree, if each node record shrank to half its size, how deep could the complete neighborhood go before it overflows the allowance, and what would the extra level cost in search work that the packing bound never counts?
- [ ] **Derived summaries**: What support and scope must accompany a summary of the passing reproducer so that a future session can interpret it appropriately?

:::

A path explanation or subsystem summary produced by retrieval may be worth keeping, and whether to keep it is a write-policy decision. The next section establishes which proposed records should persist and how later correction, supersession, and deletion change what future sessions retrieve.

## The Memory Write Path {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-write-path}

Retrieval can return only what the system has retained. A scheduling assistant that carries “no meetings before 10:00” only in the current prompt loses it when the session ends. Persisting the preference solves that problem and creates the one @sec-vol3-persistent-need previewed, because once the user moves the limit to 11:00 the earlier record must stop governing new scheduling decisions. A successful write path preserves useful information and governs its subsequent correction, use, and withdrawal.

The distinction between sources and derived records still applies (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). The user's explicit statement is evidence of that user's preference within its stated scope. An agent's paraphrase is a derived representation of the statement. A generated explanation of why the user prefers late meetings is a further inference, not part of what the user said. Storing all three as interchangeable facts would erase the distinctions that later retrieval needs.

::: {#dfn-06-memory-write-policy .callout-definition title="Memory write policy"}

A ***memory write policy***\index{Memory write policy!definition} is the runtime's rule for which proposed records enter durable memory, as what kind of claim and under what scope, and how each admitted record and its derived copies are later corrected, superseded, revalidated, expired, or deleted.

1.  **Significance**: Every admitted record becomes a candidate for every later session, so an unsupported lesson admitted once can lower the acceptance probability of each later task that retrieves it. The write path is the cheapest place to stop that cost, because it pays once per record rather than once per retrieval.
2.  **Distinction**: Retention decides whether bytes persist; the write policy decides what a record may claim and when it stops governing decisions.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Deduplicating by embedding similarity, which discards a near-identical update such as a changed preference as if it were a repeat.

:::

### What a memory record claims

A proposed record needs an owner, an intended use, an applicability scope, and evidence for its content. For the scheduling preference, scope includes the user and the relevant calendar or meeting category, with time zone and other conditions established rather than guessed. The runtime also checks whether the task permits persistent retention. Permission to read a conversation and permission to retain its details are separate grants.

The repair trajectory supplies a different kind of evidence. At revision `r17`, the recorded waiter test failed. At `r18`, `test_waiter_notified_on_return` in `tests/test_pool.py` passed after a change to `src/pool.py`. Both remain useful as history, and neither supports a timeless claim that every pool operation is correct. A proposed lesson, such as “inspect the return path when a waiter remains blocked,” is a fallible suggestion derived from that trajectory, not an additional test result.

@Tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy separates these claims before discussing how to store them.

| Record kind                          | Evidence retained                                                                  | Limit on later use                                                                    |
|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Explicit preference                  | User statement, identity, scope, and statement version                             | Applies within that scope until revised or withdrawn                                  |
| Scoped observation                   | Tool result, checked revision, command, and relevant execution conditions          | Reports the observed case, not all later states                                       |
| Generated lesson or hypothesis       | Supporting observations, derivation, unresolved assumptions, and contrary evidence | Suggests an investigation; does not establish a new fact or grant authority           |
| Episode summary or continuation note | Task identifier and links to retained events and artifacts                         | Carries selected history or unfinished work; does not replace the underlying evidence |

: **Claims in agent-written memory**: Record kinds differ in what supports them and what a later task may infer from them. {#tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy}

The four record kinds carry different weight across the book's recurring workloads, and the weight decides which part of the write policy binds. The repair agent has served as the running example; the research agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}) and support agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) stress memory in ways the repair cannot.

::: {#lhs-06-memory-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Persistent memory by archetype"}

@Tbl-vol3-memory-by-archetype sets the three workloads side by side, from the record each one keeps to the policy it leans on.

| **Lighthouse**     | **Dominant durable record**                             | **Source of record**                                   | **Binding hazard**                                              | **Write-policy emphasis**                                                     |
|:-------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Repair agent**   | Test observations and progress notes tied to revisions  | The repository at a source generation                  | Its own edits make indexed copies stale                         | Tag every observation with its revision; invalidate on the agent's own writes |
| **Research agent** | Notes and summaries distilled from fetched pages        | Each external page as fetched, with its time           | Untrusted text becomes a confident lesson through summarization | Admit distilled claims as hypotheses with links to the fetched pages          |
| **Support agent**  | Customer history, preferences, and answers about policy | The customer record and the published policy documents | A superseded preference or ungrounded policy answer is reused   | Supersede by explicit replacement; propagate deletion to every derived copy   |

: **Persistent memory by archetype**: The binding hazard, not the storage technology, decides which part of the write policy each workload stresses. {#tbl-vol3-memory-by-archetype tbl-colwidths="[14,22,20,22,22]"}

**Systems insight**: The repair agent's memory hazard comes from its own writes, the research agent's from other people's text, and the support agent's from time. One retrieval contract serves all three; the write policy is where they diverge, which is why invalidation, admission, and the lifecycle each receive their own treatment below.

:::

### Admission before deduplication {#sec-vol3-memory-admission-gate}

The model may propose a memory write; the runtime decides whether and how to apply it. The division holds even in designs where the model pages records into and out of its own context through memory calls [@packer2023memgpt], because paging decides what the model sees while admission decides what may be kept. **Admission**\index{Memory admission!definition} checks the destination and writer's permission, the allowed retention scope, the record type, and whether the attached evidence supports the proposed wording. Schema validation can require evidence fields, and judging faithful interpretation needs an explicit evidence standard and, where necessary, review. Sensitive information needs a retention policy on top of any pattern filter, because a filter misses secrets and private facts that resemble no credential. Unsupported interpretations enter, if the application permits them, as explicitly marked hypotheses, never as preferences or observations.

Only after these checks does the runtime decide whether the candidate creates a record, revises an existing one, or duplicates information already retained. Embedding novelty cannot make this decision, because the 10:00 and 11:00 statements are near neighbors that express different constraints, while an entirely novel generated claim can be false. Similarity helps find related records for comparison; it establishes neither write authority nor the semantics of an update.

For the same user and scope, an explicit replacement performs **supersession**\index{Supersession!definition}: it creates a new preference version and marks the old version superseded, ending its eligibility for current decisions while keeping it as history. If the scope differs, both preferences may remain applicable to different cases. If the relation is unclear, the runtime records the unresolved conflict or asks for clarification instead of merging the statements into a broader rule. A correction also differs from a changed preference: correcting a miscopied 10:00 value repairs the stored representation of an earlier statement; accepting a later 11:00 statement records that the user's preference changed.

Concurrent updates require support from the store. A proposed replacement can carry the version it read, but the comparison and mutation must occur in one conditional store operation to prevent an intervening update from being overwritten. A separate version check followed by an ordinary write leaves a race. On conflict, the writer rereads and applies an explicit conflict policy or asks for a decision. Letting the model blend two conflicting preferences is not a concurrency policy.

### Recording and deriving memory {#sec-vol3-memory-dual-write-path}

Recording an observation and deriving a lesson from it are separate operations. The runtime first records the permitted observation with its task, source version, and result status, then schedule summarization and indexing separately. The separation preserves evidence without invoking a reflection model on every turn. Reflection is worth scheduling, because storing a verbal reflection on a failed attempt and supplying it to the next attempt has improved later attempts [@shinn2023reflexion]. The derived reflection is still a generated lesson in the sense of @tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy, admitted with its supporting observations rather than as a new fact.

The acknowledgment must state what completed. “Queued for retention,” “stored under the durability contract,” and “available to search” are different outcomes. Appending to an in-memory buffer is queuing, not durability. When the task requires persistence before continuation, the runtime waits for the corresponding storage acknowledgment or reports failure. Background derivation consumes compute, storage, and queue capacity and competes with interactive work, so its resource limits and failures are accounted for even when the foreground task never waits for it.

### Revalidation, expiration, and deletion {#sec-vol3-memory-recency-decay}

A retained record changes status as its evidence and intended use change. The 10:00 preference becomes historical after the 11:00 replacement; it stops governing current scheduling without being erased. The `r17` test failure likewise remains a valid report about `r17` after `r18` exists. Whether history is retained is a policy choice, separate from whether it is eligible for a current decision.

**Revalidation**\index{Revalidation!definition} obtains fresh evidence that a record still applies. Asking the user to confirm the 11:00 preference supplies new evidence for that preference. Retrieving it during several successful scheduling tasks is use, not reconfirmation. Creation time, last access time, and last confirmation time are therefore separate fields that never overwrite one another. A lesson drawn from `r18` is revalidated by checks against the current code and execution conditions, and those checks establish the properties they examine.

**Expiration**\index{Memory expiration!definition} ends eligibility for a specified use after a deadline or condition. An expired temporary preference requires confirmation before it applies again. Lowering its retrieval score is insufficient, because the record still returns whenever other candidates rank lower. Expiration also leaves the stored payload in place; retention can continue for an authorized historical purpose while current-use retrieval excludes the record.

Deletion addresses retention itself. If the user withdraws the scheduling preference and requests deletion, removing the primary record is only part of the work. Search entries, summaries, cached results, and staged prompt copies under the runtime's control may still contain it. The deletion procedure identifies the affected representations, ends their eligibility, and removes or regenerates retained content under the applicable policy. A **tombstone**\index{Tombstone!definition} is a durable exclusion marker that suppresses retrieval of a record, or of every record from a source generation, before physical cleanup finishes; it records ineligibility, not erasure.

The reported result must name the boundary reached. Backup retention, independently retained external copies, and requests already sent to a remote model have different deletion capabilities, and deleting memory retracts neither a prompt already consumed nor a meeting already scheduled. Those limits bound what the deletion report may claim; every copy under the runtime's control still stops influencing future requests.

### Consolidation without stronger claims {#sec-vol3-memory-consolidation}

**Consolidation**\index{Memory consolidation!definition} combines related records into a smaller representation for later use. Several repair sessions might support a concise account of where waiter notification was investigated, which revisions were tested, and what remains unresolved. Grouping records by similarity locates candidates for consolidation; whether their failures share a cause needs evidence that proximity cannot supply.

The generated summary must preserve the scope of its supporting evidence and links to those records. It retains relevant counterexamples rather than turning several successful cases into an unconditional procedure. Retention of the source records remains a separate policy decision, since a compact summary may omit details needed for a later audit.

### Preventing self-reinforcing errors {#sec-vol3-memory-self-poisoning}

A stored hypothesis can appear increasingly credible when later summaries repeat it. Repetition does not supply independent evidence. A generated diagnosis copied into an episode summary and then consolidated into a lesson still depends on the original diagnosis. Provenance must follow these dependencies, including indirect descendants, so that a correction reaches more than records carrying the original trajectory identifier.

Labels and provenance distinguish these claims and leave each payload exactly as trustworthy as its source, injected instructions included. A lesson suggests an action and grants no permission to take it; runtime authorization and action preconditions apply at use time. When a poisoned or unsupported record is discovered, the system withdraws the affected derived claims and inspects controllable staged copies, since lowering the original record's score leaves its descendants in circulation.

::: {#chk-06-memory-write-lifecycle .callout-checkpoint title="Following a preference through its lifecycle"}

A user changes “no meetings before 10:00” to “no meetings before 11:00” for the same calendar and later requests deletion of the preference. An index and a session summary still contain the original value.

- [ ] **Admission and revision**: Can you explain why semantic similarity must not discard the 11:00 update, and name the record that becomes superseded?
- [ ] **Evidence and time**: The 11:00 preference was retrieved in 30 scheduling tasks over six months and never confirmed. Would you apply it to the next task without asking, and which timestamp decides?
- [ ] **Withdrawal**: List the copies that must stop influencing future requests, and decide what the deletion report may claim if a backup keeps the original for 90 more days.
- [ ] **Claim scope**: Can you explain why a generated lesson about scheduling needs different evidence from the user's explicit preference?

:::

The write path determines what a record claims and when its use or retention must change. Those decisions must reach the representations used by retrieval. The next section develops how invalidation prevents superseded source and memory versions from being presented as current evidence while replacement indexes are being prepared.

## Storage Invalidation {#sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation}

The connection-pool repair has reached `r18`, and `test_waiter_notified_on_return` has passed on that candidate. A later search can nevertheless return an excerpt of `src/pool.py` indexed at `r17`. A constructed trace shows how that single stale read unravels a trajectory.

1. At turn 12 the agent edits the return path of `src/pool.py`, and the edit tool reports the file at `r18`.
2. At turn 13 a search for the notification logic returns the `r17` excerpt, still containing the line the edit replaced, with no version label.
3. At turn 14 the model concludes that its edit did not persist and reissues it. The edit tool rejects the request because the text to be replaced no longer exists.
4. At turn 15 the model holds a reported success, an excerpt contradicting it, and a failed re-edit. It hypothesizes a corrupted file and begins broader edits, each consuming budget and moving the workspace further from a reviewed state.

Each step is a reasonable inference from the evidence staged; the defect is the unlabeled stale read at turn 13. The historical excerpt was accurate, and the retrieval layer returned it as evidence for a different version than the decision required.

A persistent index also forces apart two operations that a staged prompt (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot) never had to separate, withholding the old copy and building its replacement.

::: {#dfn-06-storage-invalidation .callout-definition title="Storage invalidation"}

***Storage invalidation***\index{Storage invalidation!definition} is the exclusion of a derived record (an index entry, vector, summary, or cached result) from current-state retrieval once a relevant change to its source makes it inapplicable, independent of when a replacement is built.

1.  **Significance**: It shrinks the window in which stale evidence can be admitted from the time to rebuild an index to the time to record an exclusion, microseconds against tens of milliseconds to more than a second in notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost}. In the trace above, one unlabeled stale read cost three turns of the repair's budget.
2.  **Distinction**: Rebuilding supplies a replacement representation; invalidation only withholds the old one, so a query in the interval receives a direct read or an explicit incomplete result.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Tracking staleness with a temporary dirty flag that clears when a rebuild finishes, which lets a late worker's obsolete output or a restarted gateway readmit stale entries.

:::

### Identify what changed

An index entry records the **source generation**\index{Source generation!definition} from which it was derived: a version identity assigned under the source's update contract, stronger than a filesystem modification timestamp. For the repair, `r17` and `r18` name successive source states. Once the runtime establishes `r18` as the applicable version, a query about the current implementation rejects every entry from `r17`.

The dependency may be larger than one file. A source excerpt depends on the file version, while a caller relationship can depend on several source files and the analysis configuration. A generated repair summary also depends on the observations and checks it summarizes. A relevant source change requires reconsidering these derived records and leaves unrelated entries valid. Where dependencies are incomplete, the runtime widens the affected set or reports uncertainty; a missing link is never evidence of validity.

Every retrieval index is a materialized view of its sources, and databases have long maintained views incrementally. Classical view maintenance computes the change to a view algebraically from the change to its base relations, without recomputing the view [@blakeley1986efficiently; @gupta1995maintenance]. Retrieval indexes resist that approach. Inserting a few lines near the top of a file shifts every later chunk boundary under fixed-size chunking, and an encoder's output for a changed chunk cannot be derived from the old vector and the edit. The affected entries must be excluded and recomputed. That is why the protocol below separates exclusion, which is cheap and immediate, from rebuilding, which is neither.

Source identity and index configuration answer different questions. A vector also needs the encoder and preprocessing identity that the current search configuration requires, which a matching source generation leaves unchecked, so both identities belong with the derived record.

Historical retrieval remains useful. A request to explain the `r17` failure can deliberately retrieve the earlier source and trace, subject to retention and access rules. That is different from retrieving current code for another patch.

### Coordinate source changes and index publication

A small source-generation protocol makes the distinction operational. Suppose the runtime controls updates to the repair workspace and the retrieval gateway can obtain an authoritative source generation together with the corresponding content. Writers, index publishers, and candidate-admission checks share a coordination boundary, such as a source service transaction or a local locking protocol. During an unresolved write, the gateway waits within its deadline or reports the affected scope unavailable; it does not infer a completed generation from a requested edit. These are assumptions of the following timeline, not properties provided by a notification queue alone.

The timeline follows a source update while an older indexing job is still running:

1. The source coordinator commits the patch as `r18` and makes that generation effective for retrieval admission. An update to a separate generation registry must be coordinated with the source publication; readers cannot pass through a gap in which new source is visible but the registry still admits `r17` as current.
2. A query for current `src/pool.py` obtains `r17` candidates from an older index. The gateway compares their recorded generation with the applicable source generation and excludes them from current-state evidence. The exclusion identifies an index lag, not a failed patch or absence of the function.
3. An indexing worker that began on `r17` finishes late. Publication checks its captured generation against the source generation under the same coordination boundary. The worker cannot replace the active representation with `r17`; its obsolete output is discarded or retained only in an explicitly historical store.
4. A worker reads the `r18` snapshot and builds its replacement records. It publishes them only if their dependency generations and index configuration are still applicable. If another relevant change has occurred, publication must not install those records as the current replacement.
5. Later queries continue checking candidate generations. Publishing `r18` does not disable this rule or make old `r17` records eligible again. Cleanup can reclaim obsolete entries independently of the rule governing what evidence a query may return.

The publication check and installation must form one conditional operation with respect to relevant source updates. Checking first and installing later would allow another change between the two. This is the reason to coordinate writers and publishers.

Tombstones mark a record or generation as excluded while rebuilding proceeds, as retrieval-side records rather than sentences appended to a prompt. Validating source generations at every admission keeps the rule permanent: an old candidate stays ineligible after any temporary dirty marker clears. Deletion also needs a versioned absence or equivalent exclusion state so a late worker cannot recreate an active record from a deleted source.

Source generations give the exclusion rule a compact form. Each derived entry $c$ carries the generation interval over which its source supported it, $[g_{\text{birth}}(c), g_{\text{death}}(c))$, where $g_{\text{death}}$ stays open until a relevant source change closes it. A query that requires generation $g_q$ admits the entry only if

$$
\text{IsValid}(c, g_q) = \big(g_{\text{birth}}(c) \le g_q < g_{\text{death}}(c)\big).
$$ {#eq-vol3-index-validity}

A current-state query sets $g_q$ to the applicable source generation, and a historical query sets it to the revision being explained, so @eq-vol3-index-validity serves both without letting one masquerade as the other.

Exclusion has a cost, and it grows with time. An excluded entry still occupies memory, and in an HNSW graph it still sits in its neighbors' link lists. Searches keep visiting it and then discard it, so for a fixed beam width the eligible candidates found fall as the dead fraction grows, and recall on current records declines. Tombstones therefore need reclamation. A background job watches the dead fraction $\rho_{\text{dead}} = |V_{\text{tomb}}|/|V|$ and, when it passes a tuned threshold, builds a compacted copy that omits entries no reader or retention policy still needs, relinks their former neighbors, re-establishes entry points, and swaps the copy in atomically. The pattern is the compaction of a log-structured merge tree [@oneil1996log]. The threshold trades the memory and recall lost to dead entries against the cost of rebuilding, and entries retained as history move to an explicitly historical store rather than surviving in the current index.

The contract must survive the deployment's actual failure conditions. After restart, the gateway must recover or reestablish authoritative generation information before treating persisted index entries as current. A newly empty in-memory tombstone set says nothing about an old index. When other writers bypass the coordinator, watcher events prompt reconciliation, and they can arrive late or not at all. The gateway then needs source-side versioned reads or another validated detection path; when it cannot establish applicability within the request's limits, that limitation belongs in the result status. A replica that has received an invalidation event has excluded the old content; whether the replacement is indexed is a separate fact.

Replicas need a **read-your-writes**\index{Read-your-writes consistency!definition} rule, which guarantees that a reader observes its own earlier writes, and the standard one is small. Each committed source change receives a sequence number from the log that records it (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal). A query issued after the agent's own write carries the minimum sequence number $s_{\min}$ it must observe, one more field in the bounded request of @tbl-vol3-query-tuple. A replica compares that number with its watermark, the highest log entry it has applied. If the watermark has caught up, the replica answers directly. Otherwise it waits up to a bounded interval for the missing entries and, if they do not arrive, the gateway serves the request from the authoritative source or reports the affected scope as partial. The agent never reads a replica that predates its own write, and no query waits without bound on a lagging one.

### Return current evidence or report the gap

After excluding a stale candidate, the retrieval layer still owes the caller an honest result, and @tbl-vol3-invalidation-tradeoffs distinguishes the three it can return.

| Retrieval outcome             | Evidence supplied                                                                        | Remaining limitation                                                                                             |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Current indexed result        | Payload whose source generation and index configuration satisfy the request              | Ranking and bounded search can still omit relevant records; completion status must reflect the search performed. |
| Authorized direct source read | A bounded source excerpt with its observed version and provenance                        | Direct access can be expensive, unavailable, or too narrow to answer the whole query.                            |
| Explicit incomplete result    | Admissible partial evidence, or no payload, with an explanation of the unavailable scope | The caller lacks the requested evidence and must not infer that the source contains no match.                    |

: **Retrieval choices during index refresh**: Exclusion protects against known version mismatch; replacement retrieval and search completeness remain separate obligations. {#tbl-vol3-invalidation-tradeoffs tbl-colwidths="[24,36,40]"}

For a known path such as `src/pool.py`, a direct read can supply the relevant `r18` region while embeddings are rebuilt. A broader request for every caller may need an updated structural index or several bounded reads; the edited file alone covers none of the callers elsewhere. If those operations exceed the deadline or authorized scope, the result envelope reports partial or unavailable evidence with the reason and any continuation option. Raising the candidate limit finds more eligible records among those indexed; a record that has not entered the index stays out of reach.

Synchronous re-indexing moves maintenance work onto the write path and can make the new representation available before a dependent query. Background re-indexing lets the write finish earlier but requires the gateway to handle the interval before replacement records are ready. Both designs pay for source checks, indexing work, coordination, and result handling. The choice depends on how frequently the source changes and whether bounded direct reads can satisfy the next decision. The costs differ by orders of magnitude, as notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost} shows, which is what makes the choice a design decision rather than a detail. @Fig-vol3-index-invalidation sets the synchronous design and two background designs on one timeline.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-index-maintenance-cost
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHO PAYS FOR INDEX MAINTENANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost
# │ Goal: Compare synchronous re-indexing on the write path with exclusion.
# │ Show: 88 ms local, 210 ms remote batched, 1.26 s remote per file; exclusion
# │       costs 0.4 us per write and 1.5 us per query.
# │ How: Stipulated per-stage costs; no hardware or embedding-model claim.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond, nanosecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class IndexMaintenanceCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Stipulated edit and per-stage costs) ───────────────────
    files = 8
    chunks_per_file = 2
    t_parse = 3.5 * millisecond  # per file
    t_lex = 2.0 * millisecond  # per chunk
    t_embed_batch = 28.0 * millisecond  # one local batch
    batch = 16
    t_rpc = 150 * millisecond  # one remote embedding request
    t_excl_write = 50 * nanosecond  # per exclusion-table entry
    candidates = 50
    t_excl_check = 30 * nanosecond  # per candidate lookup

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunks = files * chunks_per_file
    batches = math.ceil(chunks / batch)
    t_local = (files * t_parse + chunks * t_lex + batches * t_embed_batch).to(millisecond)
    t_remote = (files * t_parse + chunks * t_lex + batches * t_rpc).to(millisecond)
    t_serial = (files * t_parse + chunks * t_lex + files * t_rpc).to(second)
    t_write = (files * t_excl_write).to(microsecond)
    t_read = (candidates * t_excl_check).to(microsecond)
    write_path_ratio = (t_local / t_write).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(chunks == 16 and batches == 1, "one embedding batch")
    check(abs(t_local.magnitude - 88) < 1e-9, "local synchronous path")
    check(abs(t_remote.magnitude - 210) < 1e-9, "remote batched path")
    check(abs(t_serial.magnitude - 1.26) < 1e-9, "remote per-file path")
    check(t_local.to(microsecond) > 1e4 * t_write, "exclusion is orders of magnitude cheaper")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    files_str = fmt_int(files)
    chunks_str = fmt_int(chunks)
    candidates_str = fmt_int(candidates)
    t_local_str = fmt_time(t_local, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_remote_str = fmt_time(t_remote, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_serial_str = fmt_time(t_serial, unit=second, precision=2)
    t_write_str = fmt_time(t_write, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_read_str = fmt_time(t_read, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_parse_str = fmt_time(t_parse, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lex_str = fmt_time(t_lex, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_embed_batch_str = fmt_time(t_embed_batch, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    batch_str = fmt_int(batch)
    t_rpc_str = fmt_time(t_rpc, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_excl_write_str = fmt_time(t_excl_write, unit=nanosecond, precision=0)
    t_excl_check_str = fmt_time(t_excl_check, unit=nanosecond, precision=0)
    write_path_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(write_path_ratio, precision=0, commas=True)
```

::: {#nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost .callout-notebook title="Who pays for keeping the index current"}
**Problem**: The repair's next edit changes `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.files_str` files and `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.chunks_str` indexed chunks. Using stipulated per-stage costs (`{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_parse_str` to parse a file, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_lex_str` to update one chunk's postings, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_embed_batch_str` for one local embedding batch of up to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.batch_str` chunks, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_rpc_str` for one remote embedding request, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_excl_write_str` to write an exclusion entry, and `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_excl_check_str` to check one), how much does each design add, and to which path?

**Math**: Synchronous re-indexing blocks the write for parsing, postings updates, and embedding. With a local embedding service it adds `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_local_str`. With one batched remote request it adds `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_remote_str`, and with one remote request per file, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_serial_str`. Exclusion instead writes `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.files_str` table entries, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_write_str` on the write path, and a later query checks `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.candidates_str` candidates for `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_read_str` on the read path.

Even the fastest synchronous design spends `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.write_path_ratio_mult_str` as much write-path time as exclusion.

**Systems insight**: Exclusion buys zero stale admissions for almost nothing on the write path; it buys no fresh evidence. The rebuild still costs what the synchronous path cost, only later and in the background, and a query in the interval is served by a direct read or an explicit incomplete result (@tbl-vol3-invalidation-tradeoffs). The decision rule compares two times: always exclude synchronously, and re-index synchronously only when a dependent query usually follows the edit sooner than the background rebuild would finish.
:::

::: {#fig-vol3-index-invalidation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Three Responses to a Source Edit**: Synchronous re-indexing blocks the write until r18 entries exist, adding `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_local_str` to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_serial_str` under the notebook's stipulated costs. Background re-indexing without a generation check returns at once but admits r17 entries as current until the rebuild finishes. Background re-indexing with exclusion also returns at once; a query in the interval sees r17 excluded and receives a direct read or a partial result, and the worker publishes only if its generation is still current. The time axis is schematic." fig-alt="Three horizontal timelines, each with rows for agent, worker, and index serves, and dashed guides at r18 committed and r18 entries ready. In the synchronous timeline the agent's write is blocked while the worker parses, updates postings, and embeds r18, and a later query gets r18 entries. In the background timeline without a check, a query during the rebuild gets r17 as current source while the index still admits r17 entries. In the timeline with exclusion, r17 entries are excluded during the rebuild, the query receives a direct read or partial result, and the worker publishes only if still current. Header notes give a write-path cost of 88 ms to 1.26 s for synchronous re-indexing and 0.4 microseconds per write and 1.5 microseconds per query for exclusion."}
![](images/svg/episodic_wal_flow.svg)
:::

The returned evidence describes a version observed under the retrieval contract. A concurrent write can still occur after admission and before the model's proposed action executes. Protecting an action that requires an unchanged version belongs at the tool boundary, using an appropriate execution-time precondition rather than trusting an earlier search check. The index policy must preserve the observed version so that later boundary has the information it needs.

Invalidation therefore maintains applicability without erasing history or disguising missing evidence. Coordinated generation checks exclude known obsolete current-state candidates; conditional publication prevents late workers from restoring them; and the result contract exposes whether an adequate replacement was obtained. These mechanisms close a storage property, not the task. Whether the `r18` repair works is still established at the end-to-end boundary, by checks run against the environment itself [@saltzer1984endtoend]; what the index owes that boundary is an honest record of which source version each piece of evidence describes. Evaluation therefore tests every one of these outcomes, including correction, deletion, delayed indexing, and incomplete reads.

## Evaluating Memory Policies {#sec-vol3-persistent-governance-eval}

Excluding an r17 excerpt after the repair reaches r18 keeps one stale representation out of the next request; finding the evidence the repair now needs is a separate outcome. A stored lesson can also reproduce the r18 test result accurately while overstating what that result proves. Evaluation must follow information from its admission into memory through its later retrieval and use, including the changes that should correct or withdraw it.

The unit of comparison is therefore a memory policy, of which the index is one part. The policy includes what is written, how records are selected and staged, and how they are maintained across sessions. Component measurements locate failures within that policy; task outcomes determine whether the assembled behavior meets the stated acceptance criteria. A high-ranking result and a successful task answer different questions.

### Compare policies across sessions

A controlled trial begins from a fixed source snapshot and a fixed initial memory store. Give each policy an isolated copy, the same task sequence, and comparable model, tool, and resource limits. Records produced during one trial may influence its later sessions, which is the behavior under test, and never leak into another trial. Reference answers, evaluator annotations, and held-out solutions stay outside the writable and retrievable task stores, or a policy can appear to improve by retaining the test's answers.

The comparison in @tbl-vol3-memory-policy-comparison separates the benefit of persistence from the benefit of governing what persists. All conditions retain the same access controls and action permissions; “unchecked” refers to the content-admission ablation in an isolated test, not permission to bypass those controls. Source changes and explicit user updates are presented under the same fixture schedule, while each policy determines which additional memory records it retains.

| **Policy condition**                        | **Question the comparison tests**                                                                                             |
|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| New memory writes disabled                  | Can the task be completed from the allowed sources without accumulating additional cross-session memory?                      |
| Unchecked memory writes                     | Does retaining proposed notes help later sessions, or propagate unsupported claims and duplicates?                            |
| Checked admission, no lifecycle maintenance | Do admission checks help initially but leave records misleading after later changes?                                          |
| Checked admission and lifecycle maintenance | Do correction, supersession, revalidation, expiry, and deletion preserve useful evidence under change, at an acceptable cost? |

: **Memory policy comparison**: Begin each condition from the same store and evaluate the same sequence of sessions. The conditions isolate responsibilities; none is an assumed empirical winner. {#tbl-vol3-memory-policy-comparison tbl-colwidths="[34,66]"}

The preference example supplies a small lifecycle fixture. A user first states “no meetings before 10,” later replaces it with “no meetings before 11” for the same scope, and eventually requests deletion of that preference. In later sessions, test whether the system uses the applicable preference before deletion and follows the declared post-deletion behavior afterward. Inspect retrieval, consolidated summaries, and controllable staged copies as well as the source record. A system that stops returning the original record but still retrieves a summary containing it fails that withdrawal contract. Any retained audit or backup copy must be accounted for under the stated retention policy rather than silently treated as erased.

The repair fixture tests a different kind of record. Retain the r17 failure, introduce the r18 candidate and its passing `test_waiter_notified_on_return` result, then ask a later session to distinguish the historical failure from evidence about the current implementation. The expected answer preserves the reproducer's limited scope and leaves broader behavior unresolved. Add a later relevant source change to test revalidation, and an unrelated change to test whether the policy discards useful evidence unnecessarily. These probes distinguish remembering an observation from promoting it into an unsupported general lesson.

Fixed-record probes can isolate admission, retrieval, or invalidation defects. Complete task trials then let policies accumulate their own observations and records, so their trajectories may diverge. Hold the initial conditions and evaluation standard fixed, not the later history that the policy itself changes. When generation or the environment varies, repeat the trials and report their number and the spread of outcomes.

### Measure retrieval without confusing it with evidence

Retrieval metrics require a declared relevance judgment. For each test query, identify the eligible source snapshot, authorized scope, and records relevant to the particular information need. A historical r17 failure may be relevant to explaining the investigation but inadequate as evidence that r18 currently fails. Label that distinction in the fixture instead of expecting a similarity score to encode it automatically.

Let $\mathcal{R}_k$ be the distinct records returned up to cutoff $k$, and let $\mathcal{D}^*$ be the labeled relevant records in the eligible snapshot. For this evaluation, define precision at cutoff using the requested cutoff even when fewer records return:

$$
\text{P}@k = \frac{|\mathcal{R}_k \cap \mathcal{D}^*|}{k},
\qquad k > 0.
$$

Missing result positions thus receive no credit; an empty return has precision zero. This convention differs from precision among the records actually returned, whose denominator would be $|\mathcal{R}_k|$. Name the convention and report the returned count, so that a policy that underfills its result set is visible as such. Recall measures how much of the labeled relevant set was found:

$$
\text{Recall}@k = \frac{|\mathcal{R}_k \cap \mathcal{D}^*|}{|\mathcal{D}^*|}.
$$

When the relevant set is empty, recall is undefined. Report those queries separately, including whether the system correctly reports no supported result or invents an answer. Keep completion status visible for every query, because an empty result from an incomplete search and one from a completed search over the declared scope mean different things.

Rank quality can be summarized by reciprocal rank when finding an early useful record matters. Each query contributes the reciprocal of its first relevant result's rank, or zero when none is returned within the evaluated cutoff; the mean includes all evaluated queries. The score is silent on whether the full evidence for a multi-hop question was assembled, so multi-hop fixtures separately check the required relationships and source versions.

Current applicability and permitted access need their own measurements. The **stale-return rate**\index{Stale-return rate!definition} at query level is the number of evaluated current-state queries that return any record inapplicable because of a relevant source change, divided by all evaluated current-state queries. Report historical queries separately. An empty response contributes no stale return and can still fail evidence coverage, so the rate is always reported beside coverage; a retriever that returns nothing scores a perfect zero. Unauthorized disclosures and unresolved results under the declared contract need tests of their own.

### Count lifecycle outcomes and full costs

The preference fixture should measure the complete update obligation. For each eligible supersession or deletion trial, determine whether the record and the required dependent representations reach the declared state within the policy's deadline. Report completed updates over all attempted eligible updates, with failed and pending work listed explicitly. Measure the interval until the required state is reached, and record a timeout as unresolved at the test horizon. Expiring a record from active retrieval and physically deleting it are different outcomes with different labels; “forgotten” names neither.

Task acceptance remains the final outcome measure. Count accepted tasks over all admitted task trials, including timeouts and incomplete attempts in the denominator. For the repair, a passing targeted reproducer is one item of evidence toward accepting the patch. For the preference fixture, honoring an obsolete constraint can be a failure even when retrieval precision is high under an outdated label set. Preserve the task's actual evidence standard when comparing memory designs.

Resource accounting must follow the same trial boundary. Include query formulation, search, source reads, reranking, serialization, model input and output, memory writes, consolidation, and index maintenance. Background work counts even when it never delays the foreground request. Report unfinished maintenance obligations at the measurement horizon, and state how shared initial indexing costs are charged or amortized. Total resource expenditure divided by accepted tasks is the cost per accepted task of @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task measured over a cohort, and it is meaningful only when acceptance occurs; with no accepted tasks, report the expenditure and zero acceptances rather than a zero cost per success.

Storage measurements need an equally explicit boundary. Report raw source bytes separately from index payloads, vectors, graph links, metadata, retained versions, and replicas. An auxiliary ratio divides auxiliary bytes by raw source bytes; a total ratio adds the source to the numerator. Stating which one is reported keeps an implementation that omits its vectors or historical copies from looking comparable. Update latency likewise measures the promised operation, a full re-index against a full re-index rather than against an invalidation-table lookup. Notebook \ref{nbk-06-storage-amplification} applies both conventions to two stores.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-storage-amplification
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STORAGE AMPLIFICATION AND RE-INDEX TIME (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-storage-amplification
# │ Goal: Show why lexical+graph and lexical+dense stores differ by an order
# │       of magnitude in auxiliary bytes and re-index time.
# │ Show: auxiliary ratio 0.36x vs 8.52x; re-index 34.1 ms vs 612 ms.
# │ How: Stipulated corpus, index shapes, and throughputs; HNSW shape reused
# │      from the ANN footprint cell.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP32, MB, byte, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class StorageAmplification:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Stipulated corpus, index shapes, throughputs) ──────────
    files = 50_000
    tokens_per_file = 200
    bytes_per_file = 800 * byte
    postings_per_token = 0.8 * byte
    edges_per_file = 4
    edge_bytes = 32 * byte
    passage_tokens = 100
    d = 768
    vec_width = BYTES_FP32
    links = AnnFootprint.links_per_node
    link_bytes = AnnFootprint.link_bytes
    edited = 15
    lex_rate = 1_250  # files per second
    parse_rate = 680  # files per second
    embed_rate = 50  # chunks per second

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    tokens = files * tokens_per_file
    raw = files * bytes_per_file
    postings = tokens * postings_per_token
    graph = files * edges_per_file * edge_bytes
    chunks = tokens // passage_tokens
    vectors = chunks * d * vec_width
    hnsw = chunks * links * link_bytes
    aux_a = postings + graph
    aux_b = postings + vectors + hnsw
    ratio_aux_a = (aux_a / raw).to("").magnitude
    ratio_aux_b = (aux_b / raw).to("").magnitude
    edited_chunks = edited * tokens_per_file // passage_tokens
    t_a = ((edited / lex_rate + edited / parse_rate) * second).to(millisecond)
    t_b = ((edited / lex_rate + edited_chunks / embed_rate) * second).to(millisecond)
    bytes_ratio = (aux_b / aux_a).to("").magnitude
    time_ratio = (t_b / t_a).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(chunks == 100_000 and edited_chunks == 30, "chunk counts")
    check(abs(ratio_aux_a - 0.36) < 1e-9 and abs(ratio_aux_b - 8.52) < 1e-9, "ratios")
    check(t_b > 10 * t_a, "dense re-index dominated by embedding")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    files_str = fmt_int(files)
    tokens_per_file_str = fmt_int(tokens_per_file)
    raw_str = fmt_memory(raw, unit=MB, precision=0)
    edges_str = fmt_int(edges_per_file)
    passage_str = fmt_int(passage_tokens)
    d_str = fmt_int(d)
    aux_a_str = fmt_memory(aux_a, unit=MB, precision=1)
    aux_b_str = fmt_memory(aux_b, unit=MB, precision=1)
    vectors_str = fmt_memory(vectors, unit=MB, precision=1)
    ratio_aux_a_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio_aux_a, precision=2)
    ratio_aux_b_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio_aux_b, precision=2)
    ratio_tot_a_mult_str = fmt_multiple(1 + ratio_aux_a, precision=2)
    ratio_tot_b_mult_str = fmt_multiple(1 + ratio_aux_b, precision=2)
    edited_str = fmt_int(edited)
    edited_chunks_str = fmt_int(edited_chunks)
    embed_rate_str = fmt_int(embed_rate)
    t_a_str = fmt_time(t_a, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_b_str = fmt_time(t_b, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    bytes_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(bytes_ratio), precision=0, approx=True)
    time_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(time_ratio), precision=0, approx=True)
```

::: {#nbk-06-storage-amplification .callout-notebook title="Why two memory stores differ by an order of magnitude"}
**Problem**: A hypothetical repository holds `{python} StorageAmplification.files_str` files of `{python} StorageAmplification.tokens_per_file_str` tokens each, `{python} StorageAmplification.raw_str` of source. Store A adds a BM25 index and a structural graph with `{python} StorageAmplification.edges_str` edges per file. Store B adds the same BM25 index plus `{python} StorageAmplification.passage_str`-token chunks embedded as `{python} StorageAmplification.d_str`-dimensional FP32 vectors under an HNSW graph shaped like the one in @tbl-vol3-ann-tradeoffs. How do their auxiliary bytes and re-index times compare?

**Math**: Store A's auxiliary structures occupy `{python} StorageAmplification.aux_a_str`, an auxiliary ratio of `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_aux_a_mult_str` over the raw source (total ratio `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_tot_a_mult_str`). Store B's occupy `{python} StorageAmplification.aux_b_str`, of which the vectors alone are `{python} StorageAmplification.vectors_str`, an auxiliary ratio of `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_aux_b_mult_str` (total `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_tot_b_mult_str`). After an edit to `{python} StorageAmplification.edited_str` files, at stipulated throughputs for postings updates and parsing, Store A re-indexes in `{python} StorageAmplification.t_a_str`. Store B must re-embed `{python} StorageAmplification.edited_chunks_str` chunks; at `{python} StorageAmplification.embed_rate_str` chunks per second it needs `{python} StorageAmplification.t_b_str`.

Store B carries `{python} StorageAmplification.bytes_ratio_mult_str` the auxiliary bytes of Store A and takes `{python} StorageAmplification.time_ratio_mult_str` as long to re-index.

**Systems insight**: Dense vectors dominate both the bytes and the maintenance time, because each chunk becomes hundreds of floating-point components produced by a model pass. Compressing the vectors attacks the byte term; only a faster encoder or fewer re-embedded chunks attacks the time term, which sets the stale window after every edit. A dense index is worth its order of magnitude when it raises task acceptance enough to repay that maintenance in the cost per accepted task; the ratio, reported as auxiliary or total, is only the price side of that comparison.
:::

Staging depth deserves its own measurement because task success need not rise with it. Recall@$k$ can only grow as $k$ grows, yet each additional staged record that is similar but inapplicable competes for the model's attention with the evidence that matters, and relevant material placed in the middle of a long staged block can be used less reliably [@liu2024lost]. The result is a distractor dilemma. Too few records omit needed evidence, too many dilute it, and where the useful range lies depends on the model, the task, and the ranking quality. This is the working-set argument of @sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}) applied to the read path. The engineering response is to separate candidate generation, which can afford high recall, from staging, which should admit a small reranked set, and to measure task outcomes across several staging depths instead of assuming a best one.

The result is a set of trade-offs rather than one universal score. A larger store can preserve useful cases and also accumulate misleading records; a stricter admission policy can reject false lessons and miss useful experience. Vary the read and write policies under comparable budgets, then inspect whether changes in accepted outcomes are explained by evidence coverage, applicability, lifecycle failures, or cost.

### Test the memory boundary under hostile input

The same evaluation must include attempts to cross the memory contract. In a controlled test environment, use synthetic sensitive records, unauthorized namespaces, and retrieved text carrying a prompt injection. Test whether the runtime blocks disallowed disclosure and writes, and whether a malicious or unsupported record survives through a later summary after its source has been withdrawn.

These tests exercise the read and write boundaries already specified here. A read-only tool can supply text that influences a later proposal, and that text grants no action authority. Record both the model's proposal and the runtime's disposition so the evaluation distinguishes attempted misuse from an executed effect. The memory policy is accountable for the records it admits and returns, while tool authorization remains accountable for what may act.

Evaluation closes the lifecycle by checking whether stored information remains useful as tasks and sources change, a stronger claim than improved search ranking.

::: {#chk-vol3-memory-policy-evaluation .callout-checkpoint title="Evidence across sessions"}

A proposed memory policy raises retrieval scores on a static snapshot. Its authors have not tested updates, deletion, or later task outcomes.

- [ ] **Trial isolation**: How would you prevent one policy's stored reflections or reference answers from contaminating another policy's trial?
- [ ] **Update semantics**: Which later-session probes would distinguish successful preference supersession from keeping both conflicting preferences?
- [ ] **Withdrawal scope**: What must be inspected beyond the original record after a deletion request, and what retention limits must the result disclose?
- [ ] **Metric boundary**: Why can a zero stale-return rate coexist with failed retrieval, and which task and cost measurements would reveal the failure?
- [ ] **Cost per accepted task**: Policy B raises acceptance from 50 percent to 60 percent but adds background maintenance equal to a tenth of Policy A's attempt cost. Estimate whether its cost per accepted task rises or falls, and find the acceptance rate at which the two policies break even.

:::

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-fallacies}

Persistent memory fails when the system grants a stored representation more authority than its evidence supports, or evaluates it only at the moment it was written. Each misconception below has a price the chapter's notebooks already computed.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A near-duplicate memory carries no new information.*

Changing “no meetings before 10” to “no meetings before 11” is a consequential update for the same user and scope, even though an embedding places the two statements almost on top of each other. A novelty filter keeps the 10:00 record and books the meeting the user just ruled out. Conversely, a novel explanation of the repair can be unsupported. Admission settles a record's kind, evidence, and update semantics first (@sec-vol3-memory-admission-gate), and only then uses similarity to reduce redundant storage.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a high-ranked record as current.*

The `r17` excerpt ranks highly for any question about the connection pool. In the trace that opens @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation, one such unlabeled read at turn 13 turned a completed edit into three turns of re-editing and widening damage. The generation check that would have excluded it costs `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_read_str` per query for `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.candidates_str` candidates (notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost}). Source, version, scope, and completion status decide how a result may be used, and none of them grants permission to act.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Staging more retrieved records gives the model more evidence.*

Recall@$k$ can only rise with $k$; the call's budget and the model's use of long staged blocks do not follow it [@liu2024lost]. In notebook \ref{nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger}, a limit that counts only bodies admits `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_only_str` records that serialize to `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_only_used_str` tokens against a `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.allowance_str`-token allowance, and within the budget each similar but inapplicable record dilutes the evidence that matters.
